title: Abstract classes
summary: Share code between subclasses and leave a method for each of them to write.

say.never: An interface has no code at all. A normal class has all of it. An **abstract class** is in between: it can hold shared fields and methods, but leave some methods for its subclasses to write. You can't make one with `new`, because it isn't finished. Only its subclasses are.
say.bit: An **abstract class** shares code but leaves some methods unwritten. You can't `new` it, only its subclasses.

say.never: Every mechanism has a name, so `Mechanism` keeps the name code once. It *doesn't* write `getAmps()`, because an intake and a climber draw power in completely different ways. Java allows that only because the class is `abstract`.
say.bit: `Mechanism` keeps the shared name code and leaves `getAmps()` to each subclass.

steps.title: Calling a method you didn't write

say.never: An abstract class can even *call* the method it left out. When the program runs, Java uses whichever subclass the object really is. So a shared method like this works for every gadget, now and later.
say.bit: Shared code can call the missing method; the real subclass answers at run time.

steps.title: In your lesson: Calling a method you didn't write

say.never: `isOverLimit` calls `getAmps()`, which `Mechanism` never wrote. On an `Intake` it uses the intake's `getAmps()`. Then `Intake` only writes what's special about it: `extends Mechanism`, a constructor that calls `super(name)`, and its own `getAmps()`.
